blocks.text: Compound lipids are esters of fatty acids with alcohols that contain an additional group, such as a phosphate, a nitrogenous base, a carbohydrate or a protein.

items: Phospholipids are like fats but have only two fatty acids attached to glycerol; the third OH of glycerol is linked to a phosphate group, which makes the molecule polar. The hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic, while the phosphate group and its attached parts form a hydrophilic head with an affinity for water. Added to water, phospholipids form a double layer, a 'bilayer', with the polar ends facing outward and the non-polar ends clustered inside; this is the structure of all cell membranes. Some liposomes are artificial phospholipid vesicles used to deliver water-soluble drugs.

blocks.alt: Left: a phospholipid drawn as a round hydrophilic head with two hydrophobic tails. Right: a block diagram in which glycerol is joined to a fatty acid, a second fatty acid, and a phosphate (PO4) that is linked to an alcohol.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.11: Phospholipids basic structure (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.11).

items: Lipoproteins are complexes of lipids and proteins that transport hydrophobic lipids (such as cholesterol and triglycerides) in the bloodstream.
Glycolipids are lipids with carbohydrate (sugar) groups attached, found mostly in nervous tissue.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Liposomes are good carriers for water-soluble cancer drugs: a lipid bilayer surrounds a watery core, which holds the drug, shields it from breakdown, helps it enter cells and can deliver it to the tumour cells.

blocks.alt: A liposome: a sphere whose wall is a lipid bilayer, red heads facing the water outside and the watery core inside, with tails in between. Green hydrophilic drug particles are in the aqueous core; blue lipophilic drug particles sit within the bilayer. Labels: aqueous core, lipidic bilayer, hydrophilic drug, lipophilic drug.
